originalTitle: OpenAI’s Dot agent is enterprise software that can also order your dinner

content: It’s a tale as old as last week: OpenAI’s new agent platform, called Dots, is full of cute little guys who can do your bidding. But unlike the ultra-approachable Meta Muse, Dots feel very much like using workplace software that happens to be able to order you a burrito — emphasis on work.  OpenAI announced Dots earlier this week. Like Muse, Dots have blobby, anthropomorphic avatars and customizable names. In the future, OpenAI says you’ll be able to have multiple Dots, but right now you get one. I named mine Dotty McDotface. The interface looks similar to Muse’s; you chat with the agent in one window and follow its work in another as it clicks around on a virtual machine. But Dots are less personal shoppers, even though they can help you buy stuff. They’re more like coworkers: business software that can use other software. Your Dot’s virtual machine can access apps like Blender and GIMP right off the bat. You can also give it access to your own computer through the desktop ChatGPT app, and you can call your Dot if you need to work through things out loud. And OpenAI is offering Dots first to users on its highest-tier accounts, including the $100-per-month Pro account I expensed to test it. Muse and its buzzy competitor Instinct cost you nothing — at least now, and at least until Meta can get it off the ground and presumably start using it to serve you ads, etc. But OpenAI’s gated rollout says a lot about who the product is for, cute avatars notwithstanding. I’ve been testing other AI agents with day-to-day personal tasks — yielding mixed results — and I was curious how OpenAI’s bot would compare. Despite its more enterprise-y vibes, OpenAI says Dots “can do nearly anything” with its cloud computer and access to apps, so I gave it a shot with some more pedestrian use cases.  To start, I had Dot try to schedule an installation appointment for a new internet service provider at my house (you hear that, Comcast? You’re on notice). It almost got there, and even found a $100 promotional discount in my email that I had mass deleted, but got stuck at a “human check.” Which is problematic for a bot. “This particular check needs a sustained mouse hold that my browser controls don’t support,” it said. “Please open my browser here and hold ‘Press & Hold’ until it completes, then tell me and I’ll continue with installation dates.” I obliged, but it felt a little bit like some teenagers outside of the convenience store asking me to buy them some wine coolers.  [Image: I want to know how many meetings Quantum had about adding “(and not a bot)” to this pop-up. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/dot_captcha_screenshot.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] With my human ability to click and hold a button, Dot got all the way to the checkout screen, where it asked me to input my bank account details. Turns out there’s no slick Stripe integration like Muse has to save your credit card info and use a virtual card for checkout. And in any case, the new provider needed my bank account to get a $5 discount on my bill every month. Dot paused to let me enter the numbers into the virtual browser; I didn’t trust it well enough to punch in my checking account number and decided to just do it all myself on my own computer. Not exactly a spectacular start.  I gave Dot a few other personal tasks, and the results were mixed. It couldn’t find the option for a free tour and entry at a coworking space I’ve been meaning to try out, and instead offered to sign me up for a $35 day pass. I had Instinct’s agent, which I’ve also been testing, look for the trial option; it found it and set up an appointment within minutes. “Why did you miss this option?” I questioned Dot over the phone after the incident. “I jumped to the wrong conclusion,” it said. I hung up. [Image: I’m going to start calling this the Teriyaki Test. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/dot_dinner.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Later, I had it try to retrieve some information in my Ikea account about a hanging planter I bought. It reported that it was unable to log in to my Ikea account because it got stuck in a looping security check. Elsewhere on the internet, the neighborhood teriyaki spot wouldn’t allow Dot onto its ordering page. Something about Dot’s footprint seems to get it tripped up on security checks more often than Muse or Instinct; Dot offered a link to OpenAI’s page about websites blocking its cloud browser traffic as an explanation. Whatever the reason, it required more manual input and browser takeovers than other AI agents, possibly because it wasn’t purpose-built for ordering teriyaki or handling your Ikea returns. I really saw Dot come into its element when I gave it access to something fully within my control: my personal website. It is embarrassingly outdated and I asked Dot to pull together a new, more streamlined design. It did, and when I sat down to type out some changes I want made for the next version, I thought, “To hell with it. I’ll just give it a call.” I hashed out the changes I wanted section by section over 10 minutes, walked away to do some dishes, and got a ping that the next iteration was ready for me to review. Not perfect, but better. Once again, AI proves most helpful when you give it a large dataset (me rambling for 10 minutes) it can turn into something useful. I carried out a few more rounds of iterations chatting with Dot in a browser window on my computer and using voice-to-text on the phone app as I walked around the house cleaning up Brio train tracks and stuffies.  Dot made a lot more sense once I gave it access to my computer. There, I gave it two tasks: Put together a handful of video files on my desktop featuring a TV hit I did into one clip sized properly for social media, and deploy the changes to my personal website that we had worked through in a prototype. chineseTitle: OpenAI 的 Dot Agent 是一款企业软件，也可以为你订餐
chineseSummary: 这是一个上周就有的故事：OpenAI 的新代理平台，名为 Dots，充满了可爱的小家伙，他们可以听从你的命令。但与超级平易近人的 Meta Muse 不同的是，Dots 感觉很像使用恰好能够为你订购墨西哥卷饼的工作场所软件 - 强调工作。 OpenAI 宣布 [...]
chineseContent: 这是一个上周就有的故事：OpenAI 的新代理平台，名为 Dots，充满了可爱的小家伙，他们可以听从你的命令。但与超级平易近人的 Meta Muse 不同的是，Dots 感觉很像使用恰好能够为你点墨西哥卷饼的工作场所软件——强调工作。  OpenAI 本周早些时候发布了 Dots。与 Muse 一样，Dots 也有斑点、拟人化的头像和可自定义的名称。 OpenAI 表示，未来你将能够拥有多个 Dot，但现在你只有一个。我把我的名字命名为Dotty McDotface。界面看起来与 Muse 类似；您可以在一个窗口中与代理聊天，并在代理在虚拟机上点击时在另一个窗口中跟踪其工作。但 Dots 并不是私人购物者，尽管他们可以帮助你买东西。他们更像是同事：可以使用其他软件的商业软件。您的 Dot 虚拟机可以立即访问 Blender 和 GIMP 等应用程序。您还可以通过桌面 ChatGPT 应用程序让它访问您自己的计算机，如果您需要大声解决问题，您可以致电您的 Dot。 OpenAI 首先向其最高级别账户的用户提供 Dots，其中包括我用于测试的每月 100 美元的 Pro 账户。 Muse 及其热门竞争对手 Instinct 不会让你花费任何成本——至少现在是这样，至少在 Meta 能够将其付诸实践并可能开始使用它为你提供广告等之前。但 OpenAI 的封闭式推出充分说明了该产品的适用人群，尽管有可爱的化身。我一直在用日常个人任务测试其他人工智能代理，结果好坏参半，我很好奇 OpenAI 的机器人会如何比较。尽管 OpenAI 更具企业风格，但 OpenAI 表示 Dots 可以通过其云计算机和应用程序访问“几乎可以做任何事情”，所以我与一些更普通的我们一起尝试了一下
